title: Canada: Project Magnet and Sky Canada
notes: Wilbert Smith, Project Magnet and the 2023-26 Sky Canada work.

lead.text: Canada's government record on UFOs runs from Project Magnet, a Department of Transport engineer's 1950 study of whether UFOs could draw propulsion from the Earth's magnetic field, to the 2025 Sky Canada Project, a federal science review that found reports scattered across departments and recommended a dedicated public service.

summary.text: In 1950 the Department of Transport let its engineer Wilbert Smith do part-time research on magnetic propulsion; Smith widened Project Magnet to test the validity of UFO observations, including a balloon launched over Ottawa and an observatory outside the capital, and carried on privately after the department ended the project in 1954.

Alongside it the Defence Research Board ran Project Second Storey, a committee chaired by the astronomer Peter Millman that met six times between 1952 and 1954; Smith reported Magnet's findings to it.
The surviving files, over 15,000 pages from 1947 to 1995 received mainly from National Defence, Transport, the National Research Council and the RCMP, are held by Library and Archives Canada.

In June 2025 the Office of the Chief Science Advisor, under Mona Nemer, published the Sky Canada report with fourteen recommendations, spurred by public interest and by developments abroad, particularly in the United States. On the board's reading, Magnet's place in a civil transport ministry is why its paper trail reached an open archive.

record.text: Smith's 1952 Project Magnet report describes objects a hundred feet or more across, travelling at several thousand miles per hour, and concludes that unless some terrestrial nation's technology is far more advanced than known, the vehicles are probably extra-terrestrial. It recommends a substantial effort to acquire as much of the technology as possible.

Library and Archives Canada quotes Smith's 1950 Geo-Magnetics memorandum, which it presents as the origin of the project: the existence of a different technology is borne out by investigations then being carried on into flying saucers, and the correlation with his theory checks too closely to be coincidence.

LAC cites the Project Magnet and Second Storey files at RG 24, acc. 83-84/167, box 7523, file DRBS 3800-10-1, pt. 1. Its records also show a 1959-1960 Canada-US agreement creating the joint Cirvis/Merint reporting system for UFOs, and a 1961 National Defence memo whose first typical question was whether unsolved reports were kept from the press and public.

The Sky Canada report finds UAP reports scattered across government and non-government bodies, with most departments not compiling them; the RCMP has no formal policy and files such reports as non-criminal incidents, so it could give no statistics. Transport Canada's CADORS system is where pilot and public sightings land.

The report cites public estimates of 600 to 1,000 sightings a year in Canada, and a survey in which one in four respondents said they had seen a UAP, only 10% had reported it, and 40% would not know whom to contact.

Its recommendations are to name a lead department, to set up a dedicated service that collects testimony, investigates and posts its analyses publicly, to have Transport Canada and NAV CANADA encourage pilots, cabin crew and controllers to report without fear of stigma, and to partner with AARO and NASA, GEIPAN in France and SEFAA in Chile.

The report examines the foreign models in detail: GEIPAN's three staff and more than 20 trained volunteers under CNES, SEFAA's place inside Chile's civil aviation directorate and its monthly case reports, and AARO's second report. It also works the Library and Archives holding, from Project Magnet to the NRC transfer of 1995.
The report states that it was not meant to collect first-hand data such as photos or testimony, nor to prove or disprove extraterrestrial life or visitors.

A secret Privy Council memorandum of 14 February 2023 records that full exploitation of UAP #20, engaged by the United States on 10 February, was not complete, that the Yukon object, UAP #23, remained unverified as to function, propulsion or national affiliation, and that it was unknown whether it posed an armed threat or could collect intelligence.

claimed.text: A secondary account says Smith learned at the 1950 NARBA conference from the US scientist Robert Sarbacher that Americans believed flying saucers were real and that their investigation, led by Vannevar Bush, was classified above the hydrogen bomb; Smith's memo of 21 November 1950 was then classified Top Secret until 1969. The Ottawa node carries the memorandum's H-bomb statement at Tier 1.

In a signed 1983 letter to William Steinman, Sarbacher wrote that von Neumann and Bush were definitely involved and that he thought Oppenheimer was too, that recovered materials were reported to be extremely light and very tough, and that he had the impression the aliens were built like certain insects. He also wrote that he could not personally attend the meetings, so these are impressions relayed to him.

Later accounts relay further roles at second hand: Jesse Michels, relaying David Grusch, named Sarbacher and Oppenheimer as setters of UFO secrecy protocols, with no document cited on air; Michels also said Sarbacher told Stanton Friedman that Karl Compton was briefed on UFO technology in 1950.

On Shag Harbour, 4 October 1967, secondary accounts say the Halifax rescue centre telexed the RCAF Air Desk that all conventional explanations had been dismissed and labelled it a UFO report, and that the Air Desk recommended an underwater search; a newspaper quoted an Air Desk officer calling it one of the few cases where they might get something concrete.
Kevin Randle, more sceptical about Roswell than he was, says Shag Harbour is one of two cases he still regards as possibly a genuine crash.

contested.text: Second Storey, the defence committee Smith reported to, concluded that UFOs posed no security threat and were of no scientific interest, and recommended ending all military investigation; it did not investigate sightings itself.

The foreign models Sky Canada held up explain most of what they receive: it records that 174 cases in AARO's second report were resolved as balloons, birds, drones, satellites and aircraft, and that only 3.2% of GEIPAN's 3,188 cases remained unidentified after investigation.
Navy divers searched the seafloor off Shag Harbour for three days and the final report says no trace of an object was found; a follow-up press report said the Navy found not a clue.
The Smith-Sarbacher chain rests on one opened document: Smith's 1950 memorandum was not obtained from Library and Archives Canada, and Sarbacher's own 1983 letter says he did not attend.

The 1983 letter has problems of its own: it places the Research and Development Board under Compton during the Eisenhower administration, though the board was abolished in 1953 and Compton chaired it under Truman; its postscript is missing from the typed transcript bound with it; and the only reachable copy is a facsimile hosted by an advocacy publisher, not an archive.
On the board's reading, the claim that Sarbacher consulted for the Research and Development Board has no primary record and traces only to Smith's notes and Sarbacher's own letter.

questions: Where exactly is Smith's 21 November 1950 memorandum filed at Library and Archives Canada, and does the widely reproduced four-point passage match it?
Did Sarbacher ever confirm in writing what Smith recorded him as saying in 1950?
Has the Government of Canada acted on any Sky Canada recommendation, or named a lead department?
What did the full exploitation of the object shot down on 10 February 2023 find, and was the Yukon object ever identified?
Does any Canadian military record of the Shag Harbour search survive beyond the press accounts and the final report?
